title: Nussbaum
keyWorks: The Fragility of Goodness: Luck and Ethics in Greek Tragedy and Philosophy (1986)
Love's Knowledge: Essays on Philosophy and Literature (1990)
The Therapy of Desire: Theory and Practice in Hellenistic Ethics (1994)
Upheavals of Thought: The Intelligence of Emotions (2001)
Hiding from Humanity: Disgust, Shame, and the Law (2004)
Anger and Forgiveness: Resentment, Generosity, Justice (2016)
The Monarchy of Fear: A Philosopher Looks at Our Political Crisis (2018)
summary: Martha Nussbaum (b. 1947) is an American philosopher who works on ancient thought, ethics and law. She shows that a good human life is inevitably vulnerable: it depends on luck, on other people and on the body. Together with the economist Amartya Sen, Nussbaum developed the “capabilities approach” — an account of the basic capabilities every person needs in order to live a life of dignity — and she has written extensively about how emotions shape our personal and public lives.
onEmotions: Nussbaum's central idea is that emotions are not blind forces but “judgments of value.” Every emotion contains a thought that something not fully within our control matters greatly to our life: grief says “I have lost someone infinitely dear to me,” fear says “something I care about is under threat.” That is why emotions have their own intelligence — they can be understood and examined. Nussbaum argues against the Stoics, who wanted to be free of emotion: for her, emotions are an acknowledgment of our vulnerability and our attachments, without which life would be poorer. At the same time she carefully analyzes the dangerous emotions — disgust, primitive shame, anger's wish for payback, and fear — and shows how they grow out of the wish not to be vulnerable.

anxiety.text: "What is it here that matters so much to me?" — Martha Nussbaum would ask this of any emotion. For her, emotions are not blind jolts but "judgements of value": each contains the thought that something important for your life lies beyond your control. Anxiety is exhausting; it is a blurred form of fear: you sense that something dear is under threat but can't say exactly what, or where trouble will come from. In "The Monarchy of Fear" Nussbaum writes that fear is our earliest emotion: it comes from infant helplessness, and adults carry its trace. Anxiety, then, is not a malfunction but a sign that you have something to protect. When you manage to name that value, anxiety usually becomes more concrete and quieter.
anxiety.practice: Finish the sentence: "I'm anxious because I hold dear…" — and name one specific thing or person.

fear.text: The monarch among feelings, for Nussbaum, is fear: it tends to rule over the other emotions, turning into anger, disgust or envy. In "The Monarchy of Fear" she explains why: it is the most ancient emotion, arising in a helpless infant before love or compassion. Your fear is an honest response to what can hurt. Nussbaum notes another feature of it: it narrows the world down to "me" and "my safety". She doesn't propose crossing fear out: it often points to real vulnerability. But she advises not handing it all the power and giving a voice to what widens the world — hope, love, trust, shared work. You can be afraid and still not let fear decide for you.
fear.practice: Name your fear out loud in one sentence, then two more feelings that are in you right now: love, interest, hope. Let the monarch have advisers.

sadness.text: The Stoics taught that the sage is never sad: he is not attached to what lies beyond his control. Nussbaum, who studied them in "The Therapy of Desire", argues with them at this point. Emotions for her are judgements of value, and sadness contains the thought: "There was something important to me, and it is gone or diminished." People, work and places that don't depend on us really do matter, so this thought is often true. Your sadness needn't be hurried: it tells the truth — about your attachment and about what you are able to value. To accept it is to admit that you live not in a fortress but among things that can be loved and lost.
sadness.practice: Ask your sadness out loud: "What value are you speaking of?" — and let the answer come without judgement, as in a conversation with a friend.

grief.text: Nussbaum opens "Upheavals of Thought" with her own loss: she is lecturing in another country, learns that her mother is dying, flies across the ocean — and arrives too late. Grief, she writes, is not a meaningless storm but a judgement of enormous force: a person who was part of the structure of your life is gone. That is why it is so all-encompassing: it touches not a single thought but the whole picture of what matters to you. Grief changes as these judgements are gradually rebuilt: the bond with the one who died doesn't vanish but finds another place within your life. To grieve is to acknowledge the worth of the one you lost. It is a form of love that goes on, and no philosophy should hurry it.
grief.practice: Write down one thing this person brought into your life that has stayed with you.

loneliness.text: Developing the "capabilities approach" with the economist Amartya Sen, Nussbaum drew up a list of what a life cannot do without if it is to be truly human — and one of the items on it is "affiliation": the ability to live with and for others, to be in close relationships and to have self-respect. Loneliness hurts, and the hurt is about something important. It is not a personal defect but a signal that one of the central human needs currently has no outlet. Nussbaum stresses that such capabilities depend not only on us but also on how the society around us is arranged. Your loneliness is not a verdict on your ability to love but a reminder that you are made for connection.
loneliness.practice: Think of one person you felt good with, even once. Write them a couple of lines — even if you don't send them right away.

anger.text: At the end of the "Oresteia" the Furies, goddesses of vengeance, become the "Kindly Ones" and settle in Athens — Nussbaum opens "Anger and Forgiveness" with this scene. Anger often points to real injustice, and it shouldn't be ignored. Following Aristotle, Nussbaum distinguishes two parts in anger: the pain of undeserved harm and the wish for "payback" — for the wrongdoer to suffer. The first is justified. With the second she argues: someone else's suffering doesn't undo the harm. She sees the way out in "Transition-Anger": acknowledging that something unacceptable happened and turning to the future — to what can be changed. Your anger is a legitimate signal, and it can be directed where it really helps.
anger.practice: Walk briskly for a few minutes and, as you go, answer two questions: what exactly hurt me — and what would actually make things better tomorrow?

quote.text: How outrageous! Something should be done about this.
quote.author: Martha Nussbaum
quote.source: Anger and Forgiveness (2016) — the formula of “Transition-Anger”

shame.text: An infant wants to be the all-powerful centre of the world — and one day discovers that it is small, dependent and imperfect. That, for Nussbaum, is where "primitive shame" is born, which she describes in "Hiding from Humanity". This shame at our very human limitation returns again and again, and it may be exactly what is hurting you now. Nussbaum distinguishes it from "constructive" shame, which helps us strive for ideals. Primitive shame demands the impossible — to be invulnerable. If you recognise it, you can tell yourself: my needs and mistakes don't make me worse than others; they make me human, like everyone else. Everyone knows this shame, and there is some comfort in that too.
shame.practice: Ask yourself: "Am I ashamed of a specific act, or of being imperfect at all?" If the latter — put a palm on your chest and say: "Like everyone."

guilt.text: A child who pushed their mother away in anger and then brings her a drawing — this, following Melanie Klein, is how Nussbaum might picture the birth of mature guilt. Guilt arises when we realise we have hurt someone we love and want to make it right; the heaviness you feel says that you care. In "Hiding from Humanity" Nussbaum contrasts guilt with shame: shame says "I am bad through and through", guilt says "I did something bad", and so it opens the way to "reparation". At the same time, in "Anger and Forgiveness" she warns against the wish to punish oneself: self-punishment doesn't repair the harm. Useful guilt looks forward — to care and to restoring the bond.
guilt.practice: Choose one small gesture of reparation — your own "drawing": a short message, some help, a kind word to the person concerned. Do it today.

envy.text: "If you gained, then I lost" — this, for Nussbaum, is how envy sees the world: as a zero-sum game. In "The Monarchy of Fear" she describes this painful feeling, focused on others' goods and on comparison with oneself, and finds its root in fear and insecurity. Envy is unpleasant to admit, but everyone feels it. Nussbaum distinguishes it from "emulation" — the wish to become like the other without taking anything from them. If you look closely, envy shows what you value. You can keep that knowledge for yourself and set aside the hostility towards the other person. Nussbaum believes another's success can teach, not only wound.
envy.practice: Imagine that the good you envy belongs to both of you — and nothing was taken from the other person. What would you then want to do for yourself, today?

emptiness.text: The Stoics dreamed of "apatheia" — freedom from the passions — and Nussbaum shows in "The Therapy of Desire" that a life without attachments is not serene but impoverished. Emptiness resembles this poverty, only not chosen by you: things are there, but their value can't be felt, the judgements about what matters seem to have fallen silent. It is a quiet but heavy state, and hard to explain to others. Yet Nussbaum also writes, in "The Fragility of Goodness", about how vulnerable attachments are. Perhaps emptiness is not your absence but a breathing space after valuing became painful. The values haven't disappeared; they need time and gentleness to respond again. Nussbaum would not rush you: rebuilding values takes time.
emptiness.practice: Step outside or go to a window for a few minutes and wait for one small thing that stirs something, even for a second: a smell, a sound, a face. That is enough.

confusion.text: "Finely aware and richly responsible" — Nussbaum took these words of Henry James as the title of one of the essays in "Love's Knowledge": this is how she describes a person who can see complexity without simplifying it. Being at a loss is natural when life takes an unexpected turn and the old maps stop working. Following Aristotle, Nussbaum holds that practical wisdom is not a set of ready-made rules but "perception": the ability to see attentively the particulars of a concrete situation. Confusion, then, is not a failure but an honest admission that the situation is more complex than ready answers. The way out is not a quick conclusion but patient attention to detail: what is really happening here, and what matters to me.
confusion.practice: Imagine your situation as a scene from a Henry James novel: who is in it, what each person feels, what is at stake. Which detail would the narrator notice first?

quote.text: Emotions shape the landscape of our mental and social lives. Like the “geological upheavals” a traveler might discover in a landscape where yesterday was only flat ground, they mark our lives as uneven, uncertain, and prone to reversal.
quote.author: Martha Nussbaum

fatigue.text: "A needy animal" — this is what Nussbaum, without any offence, calls a human being: we have a body that needs rest, sleep and care. So tiredness is not laziness or a flaw of character. In "Hiding from Humanity" she shows how often people are ashamed of this bodily vulnerability and dream of being tireless, like machines. Her list of central human capabilities includes both health and "play" — the ability to laugh, rest and enjoy leisure. This is not a pleasant extra to life but part of it. Fatigue is the body's legitimate message about its limits, not a reason for self-reproach. Letting yourself rest means recognising yourself as a living being, not a tool.
fatigue.practice: Give yourself five minutes of "play" — an item from Nussbaum's list: with no use or aim, doodle, sing along to a song, play with the cat.

boredom.text: In Henry James's "The Golden Bowl", which Nussbaum analysed more than once, an entire drama hangs on a barely visible crack in a crystal bowl. For her it is an example of "attentive perception" — the ability to notice the fine details of people and things. Boredom can be agonising, and there is no need to be ashamed of it. Nussbaum hardly wrote about boredom directly, but her list of central capabilities includes "senses, imagination and thought", as well as "play". If we carry her thought further, boredom is a signal that these abilities currently have nothing to do. Attention can bring even the familiar back to life. Boredom is a verdict neither on you nor on the world; it may be an invitation to look more closely or to let yourself play.
boredom.practice: Choose one object near you and describe it out loud in as much detail as James would: its colour, tiny cracks, history. What new thing did you notice?

joy.text: Pindar compared human excellence to a vine fed by the dew — Nussbaum opens "The Fragility of Goodness" with this image. The good things in life — love, friendship, a shared undertaking that succeeds — grow like a plant: they depend on weather, luck and other people, and so they are fragile. Joy, for Nussbaum, is a judgement that something truly valuable has happened. And fragility doesn't cancel the value but often makes it up: we rejoice in what might not have happened. So there's no need to hold joy back for fear of losing it, or to devalue it with "this won't last". You can simply admit: right now I've been lucky, and it's worth living to the full.
joy.practice: Pause for a minute and look around: who and what had a part in your joy — people, chance, the weather? Give each of them a silent nod.

love.text: In Plato's "Symposium" love climbs a ladder — from one beautiful person to beauty in general, where nothing can wound any more. Nussbaum suggests climbing down from that ladder. What she values is love for a particular, irreplaceable person — with all their peculiarities, separateness and freedom. Love is one of the most important and most vulnerable feelings, and it gives knowledge: through it we see the other and ourselves more clearly. Such love inevitably makes us vulnerable, but this vulnerability is not a mistake; it is the price of being open. Let yourself love without demanding guarantees from love. Nussbaum calls this "love's knowledge": seeing a person as they are, not as it is convenient to see them.
love.practice: Look at the person you love — in person or in a photo — and find three traits that only they have. Let your gaze rest on each.

gratitude.text: The Stoics dreamed of making a person an impregnable fortress that needs no one; Nussbaum notes that in such a fortress there would be no one to thank. Gratitude contains a judgement: someone else has done something valuable for my life. It is an acknowledgement of dependence, and for Nussbaum dependence is part of ordinary human life: we are beings who need others. True, in "Anger and Forgiveness" she warns that in close relationships it's better not to "keep score" — of grievances or of favours. Living gratitude is not a debt to be repaid but joy that you are not alone and that goodness really happens. And the very judgement "I was helped" already brings you closer to people.
gratitude.practice: Tell one person today who makes your life better what exactly they have done for you — in one sentence, without "well, you know".

hope.text: Martin Luther King's "I Have a Dream" speech begins in bitterness — with a cheque that America returned marked "insufficient funds" — and then turns towards hope; Nussbaum analyses this turn as a model. In "The Monarchy of Fear" she writes that hope and fear are twins: both arise when the outcome of something important is unknown. But fear contracts, while hope widens the world and pushes towards action. Following Kant, Nussbaum speaks of hope as a practical stance: not a forecast that all will be well but a choice to live as if the good were possible. It is sustained by "practices" — art, friendship, shared work. Your hope is not naivety but a way of holding on to what is dear to you.
hope.practice: Do one small thing today "on behalf of" what you hope for — even if it's just one call or one page read.

nostalgia.text: A piece of madeleine soaked in tea gives Proust's narrator back all of Combray; Nussbaum, an attentive reader of Proust, would see in this how a feeling keeps knowledge of what is valuable. Nostalgia is a bittersweet judgement about the past: there was something there that meant a great deal to you. In "The Fragility of Goodness" she shows that many goods depend on circumstances and cannot last forever, yet they were no less real for that. At the same time Nussbaum warned against idealising a past that seems more secure than it was. Gentle nostalgia doesn't pull you back; it reminds you that you know how to value — and that ability stays with you in the present too.
nostalgia.practice: Find your own "madeleine" — a smell, a taste or a song from that time — and stay with it for a couple of minutes. What of that value could you bring back into your life now?

craving.text: Epicurus divided desires into natural ones and "empty" ones — inflated by false thoughts like "I can't bear it without this". In "The Therapy of Desire" Nussbaum shares his central discovery: beliefs are hidden inside desires, which means philosophy can be a medicine for the soul. Craving can be very strong, and in itself it doesn't make you a bad person. You can do more than endure it — you can calmly examine it: what belief is speaking in it, what is it promising? Craving usually rolls in like a wave and then subsides. While you are examining it, you are no longer simply carrying out its orders. Nussbaum calls such a look therapeutic: philosophy doesn't forbid; it heals through attention.
craving.practice: Take three slow breaths and on each out-breath ask, Epicurus-style: "Is this desire natural, or inflated by a thought?" Then notice how the wave has changed.

addiction.text: For "The Therapy of Desire" Nussbaum invented a student, Nikidion, who goes in turn to the Epicureans, the Sceptics and the Stoics to have her soul treated. A good philosopher, like a good doctor, looks at her particular history and circumstances rather than lecturing her on morals. Addiction deserves the same look: it is not a moral failure, and shame is no help here. Nussbaum's "capabilities approach" includes "practical reason" — the ability to plan one's own life — and addiction narrows exactly this capability. But a person's capabilities also depend on their surroundings and on the support they receive. Recovery is not a solitary feat of willpower but a gradual regaining of freedom, in which the help of others, such as mutual-help groups, has its place.
addiction.practice: Think of a person or a community where you'd be heard without judgement — a mutual-help group, for instance. If you can, say to one of them today at least: "I'm having a hard time right now."

hangover.text: "I did something I regret" and "I'm no good at all" — in "Hiding from Humanity" Nussbaum separates these two sentences as guilt and "primitive shame". On the morning after they often arrive together, and both body and soul feel heavy. Guilt suggests putting something right. Primitive shame only paralyses. It helps to separate the one from the other: to acknowledge specific actions, if there were any, and not to pass a verdict on yourself as a whole. Nussbaum wrote a lot about how people are ashamed of their bodily nature; your body is asking for care right now, not punishment. Treating yourself gently is not indulgence but the condition for sorting things out calmly later.
hangover.practice: Open a window and stand by it for a couple of minutes, feeling the air on your face. Going over yesterday can wait — right now it's care's turn.

euphoria.text: Nussbaum took the very title "Upheavals of Thought" from Proust: emotions for her are "geological upheavals" that reshape the landscape of a life. In euphoria this landscape suddenly becomes vast and bright, and such a high can be valued. Strong joy contains a judgement that something valuable has come closer. It's worth noticing what exactly lifted you so: a success, a meeting, an idea? In "The Fragility of Goodness" Nussbaum reminds us that much of what is good is fragile and depends on circumstances — but that is not a reason to give up joy, only a reason to live it attentively. Enjoy this moment, remember what it is about, and let it become part of your story.
euphoria.practice: Write down what exactly caused the high and what you see more clearly than usual right now. You can reread it on other days.

crash.text: A life with emotions in it is, in Nussbaum's words, inevitably "uneven, uncertain and prone to reversal" — this is a property of a being who cares about something, not a malfunction. The drop after a high can feel like a fall from a height, and it really is hard. In the drop, judgements of value change: what recently seemed huge and close suddenly seems distant or unimportant. But a new judgement that arrives in a moment of exhaustion is not necessarily truer than the old one. Neither the rise nor the fall passes a final verdict on your life. The drop is part of the landscape you are walking through, not its end, and you can wait it out while being gentle with yourself.
crash.practice: Tell yourself: "This is a drop, and it's a state, not a conclusion." Then wrap yourself in a blanket or sit more comfortably and give your body five minutes of rest.

panic.text: A terrified infant doesn't need arguments — it needs an adult's arms, warmth and support. Nussbaum sees in infant helplessness the source of our most ancient fear. In panic this fear rises at full strength, bypassing reason: the body seems to slip out of control, and it feels as if it will never end. Such a wave usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. The counterweight to fear, for Nussbaum, is support and presence. For an adult, part of that support can come from their own body: the floor underfoot, slow breathing, the warmth of their own hands. And if someone is nearby, you can ask them simply to stay with you.
panic.practice: Wrap your arms around your shoulders, the way a child is held, and feel the floor with your feet. Make each out-breath longer than the in-breath until the wave starts to ebb.

dread.text: Lucretius tried to cure people of the horror of death with an argument: where death is, we are not. In "The Therapy of Desire" Nussbaum examines this argument respectfully — and honestly admits that it doesn't fully console, because we do have things to lose. Likewise a heavy sense of foreboding, especially without a clear cause, is the voice of a very ancient fear, not a prophecy. In "The Monarchy of Fear" she notes that fear isolates: it drives a person inwards, and the world becomes narrow and dark. But it weakens in the company of others — in trust, in shared work. Nussbaum proposes setting hope against it: not certainty of a good outcome but readiness to hold on to what is dear. You don't have to stay alone with this feeling.
dread.practice: Say to someone you trust: "I'm feeling anxious and heavy right now." One sentence is already a step out of isolation.

fomo.text: The tragic question, as Nussbaum calls it, goes like this: is this a choice in which any decision will take away something valuable? Reading Greek tragedy in "The Fragility of Goodness", she shows that there are many values and they are not always compatible. An honest life acknowledges such losses instead of pretending one can have everything. The fear of missing out is not greed but a vision of how much of value there is in the world — life offers more than can be held. The pain of what you didn't choose is natural. But a life in which you are fully present in one thing is richer than a life in which you are everywhere in thought and nowhere for real.
fomo.practice: Choose one thing you are doing today and tell yourself: "Right now I choose this." Notice how your attention changes.

sleepless.text: Emotions, for Nussbaum, are judgements, and a judgement can be checked; only at three in the morning there's no one to check it, and it seems indisputable. A sleepless night wears you out, and thoughts in the dark weigh more than by day. If we carry Nussbaum's thought further, the "monarchy of fear" is especially strong at night: we are alone, the world has gone quiet, and the ancient sense of helplessness returns. Night-time judgements are born of tiredness and solitude, not of a clear view. Nussbaum reminds us that we are bodily, needy beings, and that is no reason for self-reproach. You don't have to resolve everything that troubles you tonight. You can simply take care of yourself, as you would of someone close who can't fall asleep.
sleepless.practice: Put a hand on your belly and take a few slow out-breaths. Tell yourself: "Night judgements are not final. I'll check them again in the morning."

betrayal.text: Euripides' Hecuba is a noble queen who, after being betrayed by a friend who murdered her son, turns into an avenger; in "The Fragility of Goodness" Nussbaum reads this tragedy as a story of how betrayal can shake character itself. Betrayal wounds deeply because it strikes at trust — one of the most valuable things we have. Trusting is not naivety but the condition of friendship and love. In "Anger and Forgiveness" Nussbaum writes that behind anger at a betrayal there is often grief: you have lost not only a person but also what you believed in. Grief, if allowed to be, frees us over time. Your capacity to trust was not a mistake, and you needn't lose it because of one person.
betrayal.practice: Name out loud what exactly you lost besides the person: faith, plans, a picture of the future. Give yourself a minute of silence to grieve for it.

jealousy.text: Proust's narrator keeps Albertine almost under lock and key, wants to know her every thought — and still cannot possess her. Nussbaum reads these pages closely: in jealousy, she writes, love, fear of loss and the wish to control the other are mixed together. Jealousy is agonising, and even very loving people feel it. The problem is that the other person is separate and free — and that is often precisely what makes them beloved. Jealousy is a signal of how much this person means to you. You can acknowledge it without turning it into an attempt at control, and ask yourself what fear it is speaking of. To love a free person is to accept that they are not wholly yours.
jealousy.practice: Finish the sentence: "I'm afraid that…" Then ask yourself: what do I need to feel safe — and can I say so directly?

resentment.text: As if someone else's pain could, like a magic potion, heal your wound — Nussbaum calls this thought a kind of "magical thinking". In "Anger and Forgiveness" she describes how an old grudge clings to a fantasy of "payback": it seems that if the wrongdoer suffers, the balance will be restored. The grudge didn't come from nowhere: you were treated unjustly. But someone else's suffering doesn't undo your harm. Nussbaum also criticises "transactional" forgiveness, which demands humiliating repentance from the other. Instead she proposes a "transitional" path: acknowledge that something unacceptable happened and turn your attention to the future. Letting go of a grudge doesn't mean excusing the wrongdoer; it means no longer giving them your strength.
resentment.practice: Imagine that tomorrow the person who hurt you punished themselves. Trace it honestly: what would actually change in your life? And what do you truly need?

heartbreak.text: "Mademoiselle Albertine has gone!" announces the servant, and Proust's narrator, sure he has fallen out of love, suddenly learns of his love through a sharp pain. Nussbaum analyses this episode in "Love's Knowledge": suffering is itself knowledge of how much a person meant to you. A broken heart is one of the sharpest pains, and there's no need to be ashamed of it. In "Upheavals of Thought" she shows that such a loss resembles grief: it takes time for judgements of value to be rebuilt and for this person to take a different place in your life. The pain is not proof that you were wrong to love. It proves that you know how to love.
heartbreak.practice: Write one sentence about what you have learned about yourself thanks to this love. That knowledge will remain yours.

impostor.text: The flawless professional who never doubts is a fiction, Nussbaum would say: in "Hiding from Humanity" she shows that all people are limited, need others and learn as they go. The feeling that you're "in the wrong place" and are about to be exposed comes to very capable people. Behind it there is often "primitive shame" — the childish demand on oneself to be perfect and all-powerful. Against that demand, any ordinary uncertainty looks like proof of fraud. But those who look flawless also hide their vulnerability. You don't have to be perfect to have a right to your place. A person who is growing is not a fake.
impostor.practice: Ask a colleague or friend when they once felt like an impostor themselves. Listen — and notice that learning is not the same as deceiving.

self_hatred.text: Compassion, for Nussbaum, is made of three judgements: the suffering is serious, it is undeserved, and this person matters to me. Try applying all three to yourself. If you are treating yourself with hatred right now, it hurts a great deal, and you don't deserve such cruelty. In "Hiding from Humanity" Nussbaum describes "primitive shame" — the demand to be perfect, invulnerable, without needs or weaknesses. When this impossible demand isn't met, the inner voice passes a verdict on the whole person. But that verdict is not the truth about you; it is the echo of an unattainable ideal. You deserve at least the kindness you would give a friend in the same pain.
self_hatred.practice: Imagine a close friend telling you these words about themselves. What would you answer? Say it to yourself, even in a whisper.

helplessness.text: In "Women and Human Development" Nussbaum tells of Vasanti from Ahmedabad in India: having left a violent husband, she could do nothing on her own, but with a small loan from a women's cooperative she bought a sewing machine. Helplessness is one of the hardest feelings: you want to change something and can't. Nussbaum, an expert on Greek tragedy, knows well how much in life depends on "tyche" — chance. We are not all-powerful, and no one is; your helplessness is not proof of weakness but an encounter with this shared truth. But Vasanti's story shows something else too: where one person is powerless, together we can often do more.
helplessness.practice: Divide a sheet into two parts: "not in my power" and "at least a little in my power". In the second column, choose one small action.

procrastination.text: "What judgement is hiding behind this feeling?" — Nussbaum would probably start with this question here too, although she didn't write about procrastination directly. Putting things off is not laziness, and behind it there are often feelings that are hard to notice. Sometimes it is fear of judgement and "primitive shame" — the demand to do it perfectly at once, or better not at all. Sometimes it is a conflict of values: this task matters to you, and so does rest, and something else besides. Nussbaum values attentive "perception" of a concrete situation more than general rules like "just pull yourself together". Once you understand which feeling is holding you, starting becomes easier: you are working with the cause, not with yourself as an enemy.
procrastination.practice: Say to yourself: "What am I afraid of in this task?" Then take the smallest step — five minutes, without demanding that it be good.

uprooted.text: What ties us to home is not abstractions but particular songs, streets, smells — Nussbaum shows this in "Political Emotions". Emotions for her are always bound to the concrete: to the people, places, sounds and habits that were part of the structure of your life. That is why feeling torn up by the roots is a real loss, even if the change was chosen, and it is lived as grief, not merely as inconvenience. Her list of central capabilities includes "affiliation" and "control over one's environment" — when these are disrupted, life objectively becomes harder. Your longing for your roots shows how capable you are of attachment — and that capability will help you put down roots again.
uprooted.practice: Put on one song from the place you left and listen to it all the way through. Then think: what small piece of that world could you create here?

overload.text: Attention, for Nussbaum, is almost a moral skill: seeing a person or a situation in all their concreteness. But attention is finite, and that is the root of overload. Every request, task and piece of news carries the judgement "this matters", and when there are too many such judgements at once, attention simply gives way. In "The Fragility of Goodness" she writes of the "tragic question": sometimes different important things cannot be done at the same time, and it is more honest to admit this than to blame yourself for lack of strength. Her list of capabilities includes "play" and rest as well. Overload is not a sign of your inadequacy but a sign that you need to choose what to set aside for a while.
overload.practice: Close your eyes for two minutes and ask yourself: what one thing truly matters today? To everything else say silently: "Wait."

unreality.text: For Nussbaum, emotions are what stitches the world to a person: through them things become important, "one's own". Sometimes these threads loosen — from tiredness, stress or pain — and the world suddenly seems unreal, as if behind glass, and you seem to be watching your life from the outside. It is a strange and sometimes frightening experience, and it doesn't make you "wrong". The world loses its colour and seems flat. In "Love's Knowledge" Nussbaum speaks of attentive "perception" of concrete details as a path to reality. The way back can begin with something simple: a smell, a sound, a touch that reminds you again that you are here.
unreality.practice: Name five things you see, four sounds, three sensations in your body. Don't hurry — just note what is concrete.

awe.text: Among the emotions Nussbaum examines, wonder is special: it hardly asks what will happen to me; it is simply struck by the value of what is before one's eyes. Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare and precious experience. Nussbaum believes that wonder takes us out of ourselves, widens the circle of what matters to us and so helps compassion even for distant creatures. In "Justice for Animals" she writes about how wonder at the lives of animals opens a whole world to us. Your awe is a moment when the world showed itself to be greater than you. Stay in it. Nussbaum believes such moments deserve room and time.
awe.practice: Stay one more minute with what amazed you, doing nothing and taking no photos. If there's a living creature nearby — a bird, a tree, a dog — simply watch it.

relief.text: The Greeks called "tyche" the share of luck on which every human life depends, and in "The Fragility of Goodness" Nussbaum reminds us that a good outcome is not only an achievement but also a gift of circumstance. Relief contains a judgement: the threat to what you hold dear has passed. It shows how much the thing you feared for meant to you, and it is worth savouring. There's no need to look straight away for the next reason to worry or to tell yourself "it's too early to be glad". Relief is a moment when body and soul can let go of tension. Let yourself live it and perhaps notice who or what helped. Relief confirms that your fear was about something truly valuable.
relief.practice: Take a slow out-breath and notice where in your body something has let go. Silently thank one person or one stroke of luck that helped.

calm.text: A fortress that nothing can enter, and a garden where everything is alive but, for now, quiet — two images of calm. Nussbaum, arguing with the Stoics and their ideal of "apatheia" — freedom from passions and attachments — chooses the second: a peace bought at the price of refusing to love impoverishes life. The calm she speaks of is not detachment but trust: you go on cherishing people and things, but right now none of them is under threat. Such calm doesn't contradict living feelings; it gives them room. You don't have to do anything with it or fear that it will end. You can simply be in it and notice what it rests on.
calm.practice: Look around and name silently what your calm rests on right now: a place, people, a rhythm. Remember it as your garden.

inspiration.text: Nussbaum, who has herself practised singing for many years, included "senses, imagination and thought" in her list of central human capabilities — the ability to create, to express oneself and to experience what brings meaning. For her this is not a luxury but part of a dignified life. Inspiration is a joyful rise, when you want to create and act. In "Love's Knowledge" she shows that imagination and art are also a way of knowing: they help us see what dry reasoning cannot. Inspiration is the moment when your imagination and your values meet. There's no need to check whether it will turn out "good enough". You can simply follow it and allow yourself the joy of making.
inspiration.practice: Write down the main thought or image now, while it's alive. Don't edit — just keep it.

schadenfreude.text: "The road of status" is Nussbaum's name for the logic in which everything comes down to who is higher and who is lower. In "Anger and Forgiveness" she shows how easy it is to turn onto it — and schadenfreude is perhaps the shortest way there. It's unpleasant to notice in oneself, but almost everyone feels it, and in itself it doesn't make you a bad person. In "The Monarchy of Fear" envy sees the world as a zero-sum game: if the other gained, I lost. Schadenfreude is its flip side: someone else's failure seems for a moment to restore the balance. It hints at where you feel wounded or undervalued. That knowledge can be used to tend your own wound rather than to relish another's fall.
schadenfreude.practice: Ask yourself: "What in me is hurt by the fact that things went well for this person?" Write down the answer — it's about you, not about them.

contempt.text: In prison Nelson Mandela learned his guards' language and took an interest in their lives; in "Anger and Forgiveness" Nussbaum sees this as a refusal of contempt — even where there was every reason for it. Contempt is a cold feeling, and it's awkward to admit. But it often protects something vulnerable. In "Hiding from Humanity" Nussbaum shows how people put others "lower" so as not to feel their own weakness: what we don't want to see in ourselves we attribute to others. Sometimes contempt reacts to real injustice. But it is worth asking what pain it is shielding you from. The feeling can be acknowledged without turning it into treating a person as lesser.
contempt.practice: Put a question to yourself: "What would I not want to see in myself of what I despise in them?" Just note the answer, without self-condemnation.

disgust.text: Slime, rot, the smell of decay — primary disgust, for Nussbaum, recoils from everything that reminds us that we are animals and that we are mortal. In "Hiding from Humanity" she distinguishes it from "projective" disgust, which is transferred onto people and groups. Disgust is a strong and ancient reaction, and everyone has it. But projective disgust, Nussbaum believes, is an unreliable moral compass: it often says more about our fear than about the other. If disgust is turned on yourself, it too may be a flight from your own bodily nature. The feeling itself is not your fault. What matters is noticing when it becomes the basis for judgements about people.
disgust.practice: When disgust rises, take a step back and breathe out. Ask: "Is this my body reacting to something concrete, or a judgement about a person?" Simply tell the one from the other.

revenge.text: "An eye for an eye" seems the most natural justice, but in "Anger and Forgiveness" Nussbaum asks a simple question: what exactly will someone else's pain repair? The wish for revenge is understandable: you were hurt, and you want justice restored. Nussbaum grants that pain and indignation are justified if you really were harmed. But the idea that the wrongdoer's suffering will fix something she calls "the road of payback": the past won't become different, and your wound won't heal from theirs. She proposes "Transition-Anger": acknowledge that what happened was unacceptable and turn to the future — to protecting yourself, to recovery, to what can be changed by lawful means. You can act for yourself rather than against the other.
revenge.practice: Clench your fists for five seconds — then slowly open them. While your palms are open, name one thing you need for safety and recovery — about you, not about the one who hurt you.

anger_at_loved.text: At the end of "The Marriage of Figaro" the Count, caught in a lie, kneels: "Countess, forgive me" — and she forgives more gently than he deserves. Nussbaum loves this scene of Mozart's as an image of how people close to each other can come out of anger without payback. Anger at loved ones is one of the most ordinary emotions, and we are almost always ashamed of it afterwards. In "Anger and Forgiveness" Nussbaum notes that in intimate relationships we are most vulnerable: so much depends on those close to us that their actions wound more deeply. Behind such anger there is often fear and grief, and "keeping score" only drives people apart. Following Melanie Klein, she writes that love and aggression towards the same person coexist from childhood. Your anger doesn't cancel your love.
anger_at_loved.practice: Quietly ask yourself: "What am I really afraid of, or grieving over, when I'm angry at this person?" When you're ready, tell them about that, not about the anger.

ambivalence.text: Winnicott spoke of the "good enough" mother: not a perfect one, but one who sometimes feeds and comforts and sometimes is late and disappoints. In "Upheavals of Thought" Nussbaum builds on this idea: ambivalence begins in infancy, and the child learns to understand that this is one and the same person — neither ideal nor wicked, but whole. Loving someone and at the same time being unable to stand them is a very common state. Mature love, for Nussbaum, sees in the other a separate, imperfect person and can bear mixed feelings towards them. Your ambivalence is not an absence of love but a sign that you see the person close to you whole. Idealising or demonising is easier, but that is a child's view, not an adult's.
ambivalence.practice: Write two columns about the person close to you: "what I love in them" and "what I find hard to bear". Notice that both are true at the same time.

guilty_relief.text: "I loved him" and "it was unbearably hard for me" — for Nussbaum these are two judgements of value, and both can be true at once. Many people feel relief they are ashamed of, though they rarely speak of it: after leaving a gruelling job, a break-up, or a loved one's long illness. In "The Fragility of Goodness" Nussbaum shows how different values can conflict and how an honest life acknowledges that conflict instead of pretending that one of the feelings is wrong. Your relief doesn't cancel love and care. It speaks of how long you carried the weight, and of the fact that your own life is worth something too.
guilty_relief.practice: Finish two sentences: "What mattered to me was…" and "What was hard for me was…". Let both remain true.

indifference.text: In Dickens's "Hard Times" Mr Gradgrind teaches children to see people only as numbers, while Sissy Jupe stubbornly imagines each particular person; in "Poetic Justice" Nussbaum takes Sissy's side. Compassion, in her view, arises when a person enters our "circle of concern" — when we feel that they matter for our own life. If no connection is felt, the feelings stay silent; this is not a moral failure but a property of emotions. Besides, indifference can be a defence when the soul is overloaded with pain. Imagination — literature, art, concrete stories — can gradually widen this circle. Indifference is not a verdict on your ability to feel but perhaps a signal of tiredness or distance.
indifference.practice: From what leaves you untouched, pick one particular person and imagine their morning — as Sissy would. Don't demand feelings of yourself; just look.

escape.text: The ability to decide for yourself what your life will be like Nussbaum calls "practical reason", and she counts it as one of the two capabilities that run through all the others. The urge to drop everything — a job, a city or a role — says that your present life is constricting you somewhere. Her list also includes "play", "affiliation" and "control over one's environment". The wish to escape is a signal: one of these capabilities has no room right now. It is not irresponsibility but information. Nussbaum values attentive perception of the concrete. Before deciding anything, it helps to understand what exactly you want to leave and what you are really drawn to.
escape.practice: Walk for five minutes and, as you go, finish two sentences: "I want to get away from…" and "I want to come to…". The second part often matters more than the first.

forbidden_attraction.text: In the "Phaedrus" Socrates, to many readers' surprise, praises the "madness" of love as a gift of the gods that reveals to us the worth of another person; Nussbaum devotes a chapter of "The Fragility of Goodness" to this dialogue. Being drawn to someone who is "not the one" or unavailable can embarrass, frighten or delight you all at once. Nussbaum passes no verdicts here, but she suggests looking closely: attraction is not just an impulse but a judgement — I see something important in this person. She also writes about the "tragic question" — when different values and commitments collide, and the conflict itself doesn't make a person bad. Understanding what exactly you see in the other and what it says about you matters more than rushing to judge.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Ask yourself: "What value do I see in this person?" Write down the answer for yourself alone.

social_anxiety.text: Everyone in the room is hiding something: in "Hiding from Humanity" Nussbaum shows that we all conceal our vulnerability, needs and imperfection. She describes "primitive shame" — the fear that others will see us as not what we are "supposed" to be. Fear of people and their judgement is agonising, and there is nothing shameful in it. The image of the "normal", flawless person is, for Nussbaum, largely a fiction that society uses to stigmatise those who are different. Your shyness is not proof that something is wrong with you but a heightened version of a feeling everyone has. The people around you are also afraid of being seen. Knowing this can make encounters a little easier.
social_anxiety.practice: At your next meeting, notice a sign of uncertainty in someone — a gesture, a pause. Silently tell them: "You're hiding too, and so am I."

uncertainty.text: The Greeks dreamed of defeating "tyche" — chance — with "techne", with art and reason that would control everything. In "The Fragility of Goodness" Nussbaum finds this dream understandable but impossible: complete invulnerability would require giving up love, friendship and everything that does not depend on us. Uncertainty is hard: it is difficult to live when it's unclear what will happen. But Nussbaum compares a good life to a plant, not to a jewel: a plant is vulnerable, but it lives and grows. A stone fears nothing, but it loves nothing either. Uncertainty is not your failure but the condition of a life that has something living and valuable in it.
uncertainty.practice: Look for a couple of minutes at any plant nearby — on the windowsill or outside. It lives without guarantees; name one thing you can lean on whatever happens.

quote.text: Being a good human being is to have a kind of openness to the world, an ability to trust uncertain things beyond your own control… it's based on being more like a plant than like a jewel, something rather fragile, but whose very particular beauty is inseparable from that fragility.
quote.author: Martha Nussbaum
quote.source: Interview with Bill Moyers, A World of Ideas (1988)

waiting.text: "Cease to hope and you will cease to fear," Seneca advised. Nussbaum disagrees with him, although she grants that hope and fear are twins: both are born when something important is out of our hands. Waiting — for results, an answer, news — wears you out: you can no longer influence the outcome, but you don't yet know it, and the feelings take turns. In "The Monarchy of Fear" Nussbaum proposes giving hope a place as a practice: going on living, doing things, being with people while there is no answer. Your waiting is so hard because the outcome matters to you. That is no reason to put life on hold until the answer comes. A life spent waiting is still a life.
waiting.practice: For the time of waiting, choose one small pleasant activity. Go back to it each time your thoughts drift back to the waiting.

regret.text: Agamemnon at Aulis must choose between his daughter and his army, and either choice is terrible; in "The Fragility of Goodness" Nussbaum writes that the right response here is not insensibility but pain that acknowledges the value of what is lost. Regret over what you did or didn't do says that you care. It is a way of seeing honestly that the other path had value too. But Nussbaum distinguishes this from self-punishment: in "Anger and Forgiveness" she warns against "payback", including payback aimed at oneself. Regret can become respect for what was lost and a lesson for the future, rather than an endless trial of yourself. Nussbaum values such pain: it shows that you see the world in all its complexity.
regret.practice: Write one sentence: "I regret…, because what mattered to me was…" What does this say about your values today?

longing.text: No "similar person" can replace this one — irreplaceability, for Nussbaum, is exactly what love for a particular person consists in. In "Upheavals of Thought" she argues with the Platonic idea that love should rise towards beauty in general in order to become safer: this person is not an example of something general. That is why the longing is so specific: you miss precisely their voice, their habits, their gaze. Missing them is a heavy feeling, and it is full of love. It is evidence of how precisely you saw and loved the other. It needn't be hurried: it reflects a bond that stays real even when the person is not near. Nussbaum would not try to talk you into letting go: love for the irreplaceable isn't meant to pass quickly.
longing.practice: Recall one specific detail of this person — a gesture, a phrase, an intonation. Stay with that memory for a minute.

world_pain.text: A Greek spectator in the theatre wept over another's grief and understood that he himself could end up in the hero's place; Nussbaum sees in this a school of compassion. Hurting for the world — over hard news, wars, injustice — shows that your heart is open. Compassion, for Nussbaum, is the foundation of a just society. But in "The Monarchy of Fear" she warns: when the pain is too great, fear can contract us and turn into helplessness or anger. As a counterweight she names hope as a practice: small concrete deeds, companionship, art. You don't have to carry all the world's pain alone. You can feel it and still save your strength to do your own part.
world_pain.practice: Choose one concrete kind deed that is within your reach today — even a very small one. Then give yourself an hour's rest from the news.

rejection.text: Two feelings, Nussbaum says, are usually intertwined where we have been rejected: grief over a connection that won't happen, and a "status injury" — the feeling of having been ranked lower. The first is honest: you hoped for a connection, and it won't be. The second, according to "Anger and Forgiveness", is deceptive: your worth as a person is not determined by someone else's choice. The other person is free and separate from you, and their decision speaks of their desires and circumstances, not of your value. This pain is deep, and it makes sense. Nussbaum generally advises not confusing what has been lost with what you are. The grief is worth living through, but the verdict on yourself you can decline.
rejection.practice: Divide a sheet into "what I lost" and "what I decided about myself". Ask yourself whether the second is true.

abandonment.text: The capacity to be alone, Winnicott wrote, is born paradoxically — when a child plays alone, knowing that the mother is nearby. Nussbaum builds on this idea: the fear of being abandoned is one of the most ancient, rooted in infant helplessness, when the absence of others felt like a threat to life itself. Adults carry this trace, and it can be very strong. Your fear is the voice of that very early need. The capacity to be alone forms gradually, as we learn to trust that care will return. An adult can give themselves part of the support that others once gave, and look for reliable people nearby.
abandonment.practice: Put a hand on your chest and tell yourself: "I'm here; I won't abandon myself." Recall one person who was there for you at a hard moment.

unrequited.text: In the "Symposium" Alcibiades tells how he pursued Socrates and received only a calm refusal; in "The Fragility of Goodness" Nussbaum reads his speech as the voice of love for one irreplaceable person. Unrequited love is a particular pain: you love, and the other doesn't answer. Mature love, for Nussbaum, sees in the other a separate, free person, not an extension of one's own desires. Hence a hard truth: love cannot be earned or forced. But it doesn't follow that your love is meaningless or that you are not good enough. Love is a judgement of another's worth, and that judgement can be right even without reciprocity. Grieving for what didn't happen is natural. And the capacity to love like this stays with you.
unrequited.practice: Say out loud to yourself, in one sentence, what this love has told you about what matters to you. Speak openly, like Alcibiades, without shame.

humiliation.text: Dignity, Nussbaum holds, cannot be taken away the way a wallet can: it belongs to a person simply because they are a person. Humiliation is one of the heaviest experiences, especially if it was public. In "Hiding from Humanity" she opposes humiliation as a violation of human dignity and shows that the one who humiliates often projects onto the other their own fear of being weak and imperfect. So humiliation, however painful, says more about the one who inflicted it than about you. Your pain is real and deserves attention. But your dignity has stayed with you, even if at that moment it seemed otherwise.
humiliation.practice: Write to yourself: "What was done to me does not cancel my dignity." Read it aloud, even if you don't quite believe it yet.

body_shame.text: Walt Whitman sang "the body electric" and was ashamed of neither sweat nor wrinkles; Nussbaum holds him up as an example to a society that hides from its own bodily nature. In "Hiding from Humanity" she shows how disgust at our animality and mortality is transferred onto bodies — especially those that don't fit narrow standards, ageing bodies for instance. Dissatisfaction with one's body is very widespread, and there's no need to shame yourself for it even more. These standards are not objective truth about beauty but largely a projection of a shared fear of being vulnerable. For Nussbaum the body is not an object to be graded but a source of capabilities: to move, to feel, to enjoy, to be with others.
body_shame.practice: Make one movement that feels good to your body — stretch, wiggle your fingers. Thank your body for one thing it lets you do.

illness.text: Sophocles' Philoctetes lives alone on an island for years with a wound that won't heal, and Nussbaum reads this tragedy as a lesson in compassion: the audience sees that such a thing could happen to anyone. When the body lets you down, it is frightening and unfair, and such feelings are legitimate. In "The Fragility of Goodness" Nussbaum shows that a good human life is inevitably vulnerable: it depends on the body and on luck. This is not your failure. People are ashamed of their needs and their dependence on others, dreaming of an invulnerability no one has, but for Nussbaum dependence is part of ordinary life. Accepting help is not humiliating. Illness doesn't cancel your worth or your capacity to love and be loved.
illness.practice: Choose one small request and voice it today to someone close. Accepting help is part of human life too.

pride.text: In "Anger and Forgiveness" Nussbaum very clearly separates two feelings: a pride that needs someone else to lose, and pride in the work itself. The first is focused on status and puts oneself above others. The second is healthy and earned: it contains the judgement "I have done something valuable, and it matters for my life." You have made something, endured something, seen something through, and that is worth savouring. In the "capabilities approach" Nussbaum values "practical reason" and the ability to carry out one's plans. Your pride is a recognition that you have used these capabilities. Let yourself be glad, without playing down what you've done. Such pride needs neither an audience nor losers.
pride.practice: Write down what you did and what it took to make it happen. Tell yourself: "I did this."

melancholy.text: Nussbaum devotes a whole chapter of "Upheavals of Thought" to Mahler's Second Symphony — music that passes through grief towards light without renouncing sorrow. Music, in her view, can express and clarify complex emotions. Gentle melancholy resembles it: it holds both sadness and beauty. Melancholy is a quiet acknowledgement of the fragility of everything valuable: you sense that beauty is not eternal, and that makes it all the dearer. The same thought runs through "The Fragility of Goodness": the beauty of human life is inseparable from its vulnerability. Melancholy doesn't need fixing. It can be lived the way one listens to sad music — letting it reveal something about what is dear to you.
melancholy.practice: Listen to one piece of music that matches your mood, from beginning to end. Notice what it says about what is dear to you.
